source.authors: Gaudet K, Faraone N, Hillier NK
source.title: Investigating chemoreception and behavioural responses of Tetranychus urticae (Trombidiformes: Tetranychidae) to organic acids, aldehydes and essential oil components

value: repelled by butyric acid at 100 ng/mL (p < 0.001) and not at 10 ng/mL (p = 0.1)
method: two-choice behavioural assay: one bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) leaf dipped halfway in the compound in 0.1% v/v Tween-80, the other half solvent only, split by a 5 mm filter-paper strip along the primary vein; one mite per trial watched for 20 min
conditions: doses 10 and 100 ng/mL; n = 50 (Figure 6 legend, as returned by the fetch summary); female mites (sex stated for the solvent controls); the Tween-80 carrier was itself not repellent
quote: Tetranychus urticae was repelled by butyric acid at 100 ng/mL (p < 0.001), but not at 10 ng/mL (p = 0.1).
note: Licence: CC BY (page statement 'open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)'; Crossref lists CC BY 4.0). Read on the Frontiers PDF through WebFetch, the summariser returning the quoted sentence intact in two fetches. Name accepted in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Dose-dependent: the sentence is a repellency result at the higher dose only. Exceptions in the same section, read from the fetch summary and not as quoted sentences: eucalyptol was not significantly repelled at either dose, linalool and thymol were repelled at 100 but not 10 ng/mL, and no compound was reported attractive. Stimulus is a leaf-surface dose in ng/mL, not an airborne concentration.

source.authors: Gaudet K, Faraone N, Hillier NK
source.title: Investigating chemoreception and behavioural responses of Tetranychus urticae (Trombidiformes: Tetranychidae) to organic acids, aldehydes and essential oil components

value: mean peak electrotarsogram amplitude 0.132 mV ± 0.0223 to butyric acid
method: electrotarsography (ETG): mite mounted dorsally on a Syntech EAG fork electrode with the foretarsi in electrode gel under the recording electrode; stimuli as 0.3 s puffs at 3.54 L/min, 30 s apart, in hexane
conditions: dose behind this amplitude not seen (dilutions tested were 10 ng, 100 ng, 1 mg and 10 mg); n = 7 for the carboxylic-acid series (Figure 5A legend, fetch summary); error type of the ± not seen; amplitudes differed among compounds (two-way ANOVA F7,20 = 5.76, p < 0.001, fetch summary)
where: Results, electrotarsography of carboxylic acids; Figure 5A
quote: Butyric acid, a 4-carbon carboxylic acid, had a mean peak amplitude of 0.132 mV ± 0.0223.
note: Licence: CC BY (page statement 'open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)'; Crossref lists CC BY 4.0). Read on the Frontiers PDF through WebFetch, the summariser returning the quoted sentence intact in two fetches. Name accepted in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Tarsal (foreleg) response, not an antennal EAG: mites have no antennae. Butyric acid also repelled mites in the behavioural assay at 100 ng/mL (separate record).

note: Licence: CC BY (page statement 'open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY)'; Crossref lists CC BY 4.0). Read on the Frontiers PDF through WebFetch, the summariser returning the quoted sentence intact in two fetches. Name accepted in docs/views/gaps/gbif-names.tsv. Contrary behavioural result: in the two-choice assay eucalyptol was not significantly repelled at either 10 or 100 ng/mL (fetch summary), so a measurable tarsal response did not give a repellency effect here.

source.authors: Piou V, Vilarem C, Blanchard S, Armengaud C, Heeb P, Vétillard A
source.title: Varroa destructor relies on physical cues to feed in artificial conditions

value: females with the foreleg sensory pit (main olfactory organ) blocked still found the feeding site and fed
method: artificial feeding chambers (PBS under Parafilm); sensory pit on the forelegs covered with nail polish, controls marked with nail polish on the dorsal scutum
conditions: 86.4% of sense-deprived females fed (n = 44) against 81.1% of nail-polish controls (n = 37), no significant difference (percentages seen as quoted fragments, n from the fetch summary); the sense was blocked, not ablated, and the authors describe the pit as the main olfactory organ in the Discussion
quote: The mites were still able to detect the feeding site when deprived of the sensory pit.
note: Licence: CC BY 4.0 (page statement and Crossref). Read on the journal PDF through WebFetch. Name: NZOR lists Varroa destructor Anderson & Trueman, 2000 as the preferred, in-use name (NZOR prints the family as 'Varoidae', a typo for Varroidae, Plazi lists Varroidae Delfinado & Baker 1974); not in gbif-names.tsv and no GBIF page reached. Null result: blocking the sensory pit did not reduce feeding in this artificial set-up, so it does not show the pit is unused in the hive. Discussion and Results figures for PBS versus Parafilm feeding appear swapped in the fetch summary (93%/96%); not carried here.

source.authors: Piou V, Vilarem C, Blanchard S, Armengaud C, Heeb P, Vétillard A
source.title: Varroa destructor relies on physical cues to feed in artificial conditions

value: females feed guided by physical cues only (shape of the membrane over the food)
method: artificial feeding designs with PBS under Parafilm: flat membrane (disc) against a rounded bubble; behaviour scored in test arenas
conditions: in the system with no honey bee odour 100% of females fed (N = 32, 95% CI 89.1 to 100, seen as a quoted fragment); time on the bubble 55.2 ± 6.1% of 10 min (N = 32) against 4.9 ± 1.3% on the flat membrane (fetch summary); the arena contained only PBS with blue dye, no chemical attractant described
quote: We found that V. destructor is still able to feed only guided by physical cues.
note: Licence: CC BY 4.0 (page statement and Crossref). Read on the journal PDF through WebFetch. Name: NZOR lists Varroa destructor Anderson & Trueman, 2000 as the preferred, in-use name (NZOR prints the family as 'Varoidae', a typo for Varroidae, Plazi lists Varroidae Delfinado & Baker 1974); not in gbif-names.tsv and no GBIF page reached. The abstract goes on to say detection of the food source seems shape-related because a 3D membrane triggers arrestment and exploration (cut sentence). Parafilm may pass small volatiles, which the authors note, so chemical cues are not fully excluded.

value: chose the darkest grey target (G45) in preference to lighter greys
method: laboratory multiple-choice arena (glass Petri dish with coloured wall targets); each psyllid tested once, individually, for up to 30 min; Experiment 3 offered shades of grey
conditions: illumination held constant at about 5180 lux and the arena rotated between trials (fetch summary); Experiment 1 sample size for this species n = 92 (from the gender analysis; n for Experiment 3 not seen); the other grey-testing species, Glycaspis brimblecombei, showed no significant attraction to a specific grey

source.authors: Farnier K, Dyer AG, Steinbauer MJ
source.title: Related but not alike: not all Hemiptera are attracted to yellow

quote: Anoeconeossa bundoorensis preferred the darkest target (G45) to the others.
note: Licence: CC BY (notice printed on the Frontiers PDF read through WebFetch). Crossref, queried for author order and volume, returned no licence and no article number; the PDF header gives Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution volume 2, article 67, October 2014. Name: the repo's gbif-names.tsv maps the spelling 'Anoeconesossa bundoorensis' (used in earlier main rows) to the accepted Anoeconeossa bundoorensis; family, order and class follow the earlier main rows. The summariser also returned that the Results sentence on grey shades for G. brimblecombei begins 'However' and does not name the species, so no record is filed for it. Not a measured spectral sensitivity: a target-choice preference whose target reflectance spectra were not seen.
